title: System Design
blurb: Architecting things that scale — the senior-engineer skill.

lessons.title: Scaling basics
lessons.explain: Scaling begins with concrete requirements: request rate, data size, latency target, availability target, and the operations users actually perform. Load balancing and horizontal scaling add capacity, caching removes repeated work, and queues absorb work that does not need to finish inside the request.
lessons.example:
users -> load balancer -> [server, server, server]
              cache <-> database

lessons.title: Load balancing
objectives: Explain what a load balancer does and why
Explain how load balancer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect load balancer with horizontal scaling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple servers, so no single server gets overwhelmed while others sit idle. This also enables horizontal scaling -- adding more servers to handle more traffic -- and improves availability, since traffic can be redirected away from a server that goes down.
examples:
# without a load balancer: all traffic hits ONE server
# with a load balancer: requests are distributed across server1, server2, server3
# if server2 goes down, the load balancer stops sending it traffic
commonMistakes: Scaling by making a single server bigger (vertical scaling) indefinitely, instead of distributing load across multiple servers -- there's a hard ceiling to how big one machine can get.
lessons.careerRelevance: Load balancing is foundational to nearly every real system that needs to handle serious traffic.

lessons.title: Caching
objectives: Explain what caching is and its trade-offs
Explain how cache changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect cache with cache invalidation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Caching trades freshness and complexity for lower latency and less repeated backend work. You must define the cache key, what is stored, how long it remains valid, and what happens when the source data changes.
commonMistakes: Caching data that changes frequently without a clear invalidation strategy -- users can see stale, incorrect data without realizing it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Caching is one of the highest-leverage performance techniques in real systems, and also one of the trickiest to get right.

lessons.title: Databases at scale
objectives: Explain database replication and sharding
Explain how replication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect replication with sharding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Databases at scale require deciding where data lives and how copies remain useful. Replication creates additional copies for availability or read capacity, while sharding or partitioning divides data across nodes.
examples:
# replication: primary DB handles writes, replicas handle reads,
# spreading read load and providing failover if primary goes down

# sharding: users A-M on shard 1, users N-Z on shard 2 --
# each shard holds only part of the total data
commonMistakes: Sharding a database before it's actually necessary -- sharding adds real complexity (cross-shard queries become harder), so it's usually a later-stage decision, not a starting default.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding replication and sharding is essential once a system's data outgrows a single database server.

lessons.title: Consistency vs availability: making the design choice
objectives: Translate product requirements into consistency/availability choices
Explain what the system should do during a partition
Explain how consistency requirement changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect consistency requirement with availability requirement and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The CAP theorem itself is taught in Distributed Systems. In System Design, the useful skill is turning consistency and availability requirements into an architecture decision.
examples:
Design comparison:
- Payment ledger: reject/queue uncertain writes rather than accept conflicting balances.
- Social activity feed: serving a slightly stale feed may be preferable to becoming unavailable.
The decision starts from the product invariant, not from memorizing CAP labels.
commonMistakes: Saying “choose consistency or availability” without stating the actual product invariant or what happens during a partition.
lessons.careerRelevance: CAP theorem vocabulary comes up constantly in system design interviews and distributed systems discussions.

lessons.title: Messaging & queues
objectives: Explain asynchronous messaging between services
Explain how message queue changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect message queue with asynchronous and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A message queue decouples producers from consumers so work can be processed asynchronously and bursts can be absorbed. Delivery is not automatically “exactly once”: many practical systems provide at-least-once delivery, meaning a consumer may see the same message again after a timeout or retry.
examples:
# synchronous: place_order() waits for send_email() to fully complete
# asynchronous with a queue: place_order() pushes a 'send email' message
# to a queue and returns immediately; a separate worker processes it whenever ready
commonMistakes: Making every operation synchronous even when the caller doesn't actually need to wait for the result -- this needlessly slows down the user-facing request.
lessons.careerRelevance: Message queues underlie most real, resilient systems that handle background work or high traffic bursts.

lessons.title: CDNs (Content Delivery Networks)
objectives: Explain what a CDN does and why it improves performance
Explain how CDN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CDN with edge server and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CDN caches and serves static content (images, videos, JS/CSS files) from servers geographically distributed close to actual users, rather than all requests traveling back to one origin server. This reduces latency (physical distance directly affects network round-trip time) and reduces load on the origin server itself.
examples:
# without a CDN: a user in Dubai fetches an image from a server in the US --
# long round trip every time
# with a CDN: that image is cached at a nearby edge server,
# served with much lower latency
commonMistakes: Serving large static assets (images, videos) directly from the origin server for a global user base, instead of using a CDN to reduce latency and origin load.
lessons.careerRelevance: CDNs are standard infrastructure for almost any real, globally-used web application.

lessons.title: Availability & reliability
objectives: Reason about redundancy and single points of failure
Explain how availability changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect availability with single point of failure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Availability is the fraction of time a service successfully provides its required behavior, but engineering teams need a concrete target rather than the vague goal of “high availability.” An SLO states a measurable reliability target such as successful requests or latency over a time window.
examples:
# a single database server with no replica is a single point of failure --
# if it goes down, the whole system goes down
# adding a replica (and automatic failover) removes that single point of failure
commonMistakes: Building a critical system component with no redundancy at all, creating an unnecessary single point of failure.
lessons.careerRelevance: Availability and eliminating single points of failure are central concerns in any real production system design.

lessons.title: Estimating scale in system design
objectives: Do back-of-envelope estimation to guide design decisions
Explain how scale estimation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scale estimation with back-of-envelope and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before designing a system, roughly estimating scale (how many users, requests per second, how much data) determines which decisions even matter -- a design that's fine for 100 users may fall apart at 10 million. This estimation doesn't need to be precise, just roughly right, to rule out approaches that clearly won't work at the real expected scale.
examples:
# rough estimation example:
# 1 million daily active users, each making ~10 requests/day
# = 10 million requests/day = ~115 requests/second on average
# (with peak traffic likely several times higher than the average)
commonMistakes: Designing a system without any rough sense of expected scale, then discovering an approach fundamentally doesn't work once real traffic arrives.
lessons.careerRelevance: Scale estimation is a standard, expected first step in real system design interviews and real architecture planning.

lessons.title: Designing a distributed data storage service
objectives: Structure a system-design answer around requirements, partitioning, replication, consistency, caching, and failure recovery
Explain how partitioning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect partitioning with replication and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A distributed-storage design interview should start with requirements: data size, read/write volume, latency, durability, and consistency needs. Then choose an API and data model, partition keys, replication strategy, consistency behavior, caching, and failure handling.
lessons.example: Example key-value store: hash key to partition -> replicate each partition across failure domains -> route through a service layer -> use quorum/leader rules for writes -> cache hot reads -> monitor imbalance and rebalance partitions when nodes are added.
commonMistakes: Starting with a technology list before clarifying requirements.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

exercises.title: Diagnose a system slowing down under load
exercises.prompt: An API's response times were fine at low traffic but degrade sharply once daily active users doubled. CPU on the app servers looks fine, but database query times have spiked. What's your first hypothesis, and what would you check next?
exercises.hint: likely the database itself is the bottleneck (missing index, no read replicas, or connection pool exhaustion) -- check slow query logs and connection pool metrics before assuming it's the app layer

exercises.title: Diagnose a cascading failure
exercises.prompt: One backend service starts timing out. Within minutes, three unrelated-seeming services also start failing. What architectural issue would you suspect, and what pattern prevents this?
exercises.hint: likely a lack of timeouts/circuit breakers -- callers waiting indefinitely on the failing service exhaust their own resources (threads/connections), causing the failure to cascade; circuit breakers and sensible timeouts contain this

description: Architecting things that scale — the senior-engineer skill.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you start a system design interview when given a vague prompt like 'design Twitter'?
interviewPreparation.a: Clarify requirements and scope first -- what's the actual scale (users, requests/second), which features matter most (posting, reading a feed, search), and what constraints exist (consistency requirements, latency budget). Jumping straight to a diagram without this context usually leads to designing the wrong thing well.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide when to introduce caching into a design?
interviewPreparation.a: When you have read-heavy access patterns with data that doesn't change on every request, and you've identified the specific expensive or repeated operation caching would avoid. Caching everything by default without a stated invalidation strategy trades a real, immediate cost (staleness bugs) for a benefit you haven't confirmed you need.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you explain the CAP theorem trade-off in an interview, concretely?
interviewPreparation.a: Rather than reciting the acronym, ground it in a real scenario: during a network partition, do you refuse some requests to guarantee no stale reads (consistency), or keep answering with potentially stale data (availability)? Tie the choice to the actual system -- a banking balance leans consistency; a social media like-count leans availability.

interviewPreparation.q: What's a sign that a candidate is communicating well during a system design interview, beyond having the right answer?
interviewPreparation.a: Narrating trade-offs out loud as they're made ('I'm choosing X over Y because...'), checking in on assumptions rather than working silently, and being willing to revise the design when new constraints are introduced -- this mirrors how real design decisions actually get made and reviewed on a team.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you approach estimating scale for a system you're designing?
interviewPreparation.a: Start from a rough number of users or requests, and derive requests-per-second, storage growth, and bandwidth needs from there -- it doesn't need to be precise, just roughly right, to rule out approaches that clearly won't work at the real expected scale. Stating an explicit estimate, even approximate, is usually more valuable than skipping it.

careerApplications: Common in later-round SWE interviews, even for some internships.

capstone.title: Design, document, and defend a scalable system architecture
capstone.description: Choose a realistic system (e.g. a URL shortener at scale, a ride-sharing dispatch service, or a social media feed) and produce a full design document: requirements and scale estimation, a component architecture diagram, explicit trade-off decisions (and what you rejected and why), and a written incident postmortem for one failure mode you deliberately design for. This should read like something you'd actually present in a system design interview or an internal design review, not just a diagram.
deliverables: A written requirements and scale-estimation section (expected users, requests/second, data volume)
An architecture diagram showing the major components and how they connect
At least 3 explicit trade-off decisions, each stating what you chose, what you rejected, and why
A single-point-of-failure analysis identifying at least one real risk and how you mitigate it
A short incident postmortem: a plausible failure scenario for your design, how you'd detect it, and how you'd respond
capstone.portfolioTips: A well-written design doc is one of the strongest possible interview artifacts -- bring it to system design interviews and reference it directly rather than starting from a blank whiteboard; it shows you can produce this thinking under real conditions, not just in the moment.
